analysis.title: $1.4 Trillion In AI Spending, 0.2% Of GDP Growth: Goldman Explains Where The AI Boom Goes Missing
key_insights: Goldman economist Jessica Rindels estimates US AI hardware and software spending will top $900B annualized by end-2026 and reach $1.4T by end-2027, roughly 4% of GDP. The direct boost to measured real GDP growth is only 0.2pp in each year.

Real business fixed investment grew at an 11% annualized pace in Q1-Q3 2026, and Goldman expects 8.4% in Q4. AI accounted for about 6.5pp of 2026 growth and last year's fiscal-bill investment tax incentives for about 3pp. Without both, capex growth would have been about 1.5%.

Goldman forecasts a further $500B (1.5% of GDP) AI spending increase in 2027, slightly below the $550B rise in 2026. About $1.3T of the end-2027 run-rate goes to hardware. AI is expected to remain the dominant driver of capex growth.

Three reasons the spending barely shows in GDP. First, inflation: real spending grows only $250-300B (about 0.8% of GDP) because computer and semiconductor prices rose sharply. Second, imports: most AI equipment is made abroad, so investment is largely offset by imports. Third, national accounts treat semiconductors as intermediate inputs, so imported AI chips count as imports but not as investment.

Goldman says imported semiconductors used for AI make a negative contribution to measured GDP. Nvidia and Broadcom foreign revenue has risen sharply, but US exports of tech-related services have barely moved, so much US design value-add appears to go unrecorded.

With semiconductors counted as investment, AI adds 5.3pp to true capex growth in 2027 versus 4.3pp measured. The true direct GDP effect is 0.8pp in 2026 and 0.7pp in 2027. After spillovers (wealth effect positive, AI-driven electricity and other price increases and crowding out negative), the net boost to true GDP growth is 0.6pp in both years. Morning Stanley's much larger figure counts spending before netting out imports.

Goldman expects newly elected Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan, which hold over a third of planned US data center capacity, to impose moratoria on new data centers. Goldman equity analysts put 45% of planned capacity in the moratorium zone. Rindels expects limited 2027 impact because moratoria likely hit only unpermitted projects, spending is back-loaded in a 2-3 year build, and the moratoria should not last long.

Stricter or longer moratoria pose downside risks, particularly in 2028-2029, since much of 2028-2030 capacity is in the announced but not under construction bucket. JPMorgan reached a similar conclusion: 2027 is paid for, 2028 needs a permit.
Construction of IRA- and CHIPS-subsidized factories is falling, but data centers and power plants more than filled the gap in construction spending.

Higher oil prices since the start of the Iran war added 0.5pp to 2026 capex growth, with another 0.5pp expected in 2027. Goldman's commodity team says WTI must stay above $70 (about $90 now) for shale capex to keep rising.

Tighter financial conditions from higher yields and lower stocks would cut 2027 capex growth by 1.0pp if they stay where they are. The 10Y yield touched 5% on the morning of the note, and the article says AI capex is itself now driving rates.

Goldman forecasts 2027 real business fixed investment growth of 8% (Q4/Q4), nearly double the 4.2% consensus, and real GDP growth of 2.4%. The path slopes down through the year because of frontloaded AI spending.

Goldman's Delta One head cited the SOX at a 12x blended forward P/E and Nvidia at its lowest multiple since 2013, saying the market may be signaling that 2027 is a peak. Jefferies' Chris Wood argues for a peak in AI capex, citing widening hyperscaler bond spreads and neocloud CDS.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia after reports about his personal life, including a relationship with an executive tied to Singapore-based customer Megaspeed, whom US intelligence reportedly linked to Chinese state security. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO per the 8-K. Nvidia was down 7.5% premarket and neoclouds were off 5-10% per Goldman's TMT desk.
The author tracked $4.1T of hyperscaler debt and off-balance-sheet commitments last month, up $1T in 90 days. The author concludes 2027 will be remembered as the AI capex peak.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman economists forecast 8% real business fixed investment growth in 2027, nearly double the 4.2% consensus, with AI remaining the dominant driver and a further $500B increase in AI spending.
tension_points.bear_case: Spending is frontloaded and slows in the second half of 2027. Jefferies cites widening hyperscaler bond spreads and neocloud CDS, Goldman's Delta One head says 2027 may be a peak, and the funding leans on debt and off-balance-sheet commitments.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financial conditions staying tight with the 10Y near 5% would cut 2027 capex growth by 1.0pp, and stricter or longer data center moratoria pose downside risks in 2028-2029.

tension_points.bull_case: Rindels expects little 2027 impact because moratoria likely hit only unpermitted projects, most delayed spending would not have landed in 2027 anyway, and the moratoria are not expected to be long-lived.
tension_points.bear_case: Goldman equity analysts put 45% of planned capacity in the moratorium zone, and much of 2028-2030 capacity sits in the announced but not under construction bucket.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Moratoria that are stricter or longer-lasting than expected, per Goldman, pose downside risks particularly in 2028-2029.
